Day 5 of working on GPU kernel optimization for the Open Kernel Challenge.

Yesterday I finished Day 4 with a new best measured result: 1.186× SGLang, 4,072 µs, with all 9/9 correctness tests passed.

Yesterday I learned that improving performance doesn’t always mean making the main computation faster.

I spent a lot of time experimenting with custom Triton kernels to replace existing matrix multiplications. Most of my attempts were slower than SGLang.

For QKV with 128 tokens, my Hopper TMA implementation took 40.4 µs compared to SGLang’s 17.2 µs.

At 256 tokens, it was 71.4 µs versus 20.1 µs.

Instead of continuing to optimize the matrix multiplication, I decided to examine the operations around it.

In the FP32 router, the computation produced 512 intermediate values per row, but the final output only needed 256.

I replaced the PyTorch addition with a Triton kernel and experimented with processing multiple rows per GPU program.

Processing four rows at once brought the result to 1.181× and 4,089.2 µs.

Then I tried something different.

Instead of allocating a separate output buffer, I made the kernel write the results directly into the existing intermediate buffer.

That brought my best measured result to 1.186× and 4,072 µs.

Not every experiment worked. Placing the high and low BF16 weight components next to each other in memory reduced performance to 1.178×.

What I learned is that sometimes removing unnecessary memory operations can be more effective than replacing an already optimized computation.

But there’s still a problem I need to solve.

My best measured result was 1.186×, while the same code achieved only 1.175× in the official run. My best official score remains 1.180×.

So today, on Day 5, I’m focusing on something just as important as speed: understanding why performance varies between runs and how to make these improvements consistent.

▲ Prime Intellect just released Prime Mega MoE, which makes DeepSeek's fused Mega MoE kernel usable for training, not just inference.

The key idea is overlap. MoE layers normally route, send, compute and return as separate steps, so GPUs sit idle waiting on communication. DeepSeek's Mega MoE fuses those steps into 1 kernel, but it only had a forward pass. Prime Intellect added a fast, overlapping backward kernel.

On Qwen3-235B-A22B (128 H200), a training step drops from 14.98 s with TorchTitan to 9.65 s, 55% faster. Against its own prime-rl baseline, steps are 32% to 34% faster. It is a trade-off though: the forward pass gets up to 3.11x faster, but the backward pass on the 235B layer gains only 1.24x.

It ships today in prime-rl (Apache 2.0) as the mega_moe dispatch backend, with BF16, blockwise FP8 on Hopper and MXFP8 on Blackwell......

Update: I’ve been making progress on all the other kernels using fleets of agents, and discovered human-guided fleets are over 2x faster than Astra-guided fleets!

We spent ~$5k testing fleets of agents running experiments on H200s. 

Interesting results from the Open Kernel Challenge:

1) Human-guided fleets now progress over 2x faster than Astra guided fleets, and Astra alone is now too slow to make progress. Early on, human guided Astra made most of the progress based on intuition alone. 

As the basic memory and GPGPU tricks are exhausted, most of the new kernels breakthroughs come from exhaustive testing on GPUs for optimizations and reorganizations of data/code. 

So early boosts came from human insight, but now it's mostly based on how much you can spend on GPU testing. 

2) Astra sometimes makes obvious mistakes a human expert would catch, like not combining other kernels into the full decode kernels, and not submitting breakthroughs for incorrect rules.

3) The best design is having a human expert keep adding agents till they respond every 1-5 minutes, then guide them with simple quick answers. I now run 30. 

4) A human-guided fleet running Gemini 3.8 flash outperforms Astra Ultra alone and the Astra-guided fleet. 

5) We spent ~$4500 in Gemini 3.8 flash running the fleet, 30 agents in parallel, and ~$600 in subscriptions running Astra, so the fleet is very expensive to run. 

6) Gemini Argon kept stopping for security reasons so 3.8 Flash did better. 

Most of the time was previously spent waiting for experiments, so I added agents till I didn't have to wait.

I built a local queue and lock system for all my GPUs, so they constantly have 100% utilization running independent experiments from the fleet. 

Sometimes the fleet still goes off the rails, so humans need to re-prompt them. Astra can resolve some of this and verify the fleet, but when Astra goes off the rails you need a human expert. This explains the slowdown when Astra guides the fleet. 

This is strong evidence that human experts guiding fleets of agents is both important to reach out-of-distribution solutions and make progress faster(for now).

$META is making its ad engine dramatically more powerful with $NVDA help. And this could have a meaningful impact on its advertising economics.

Meta and Nvidia have been working together to optimize Andromeda, Meta's AI-powered ad retrieval engine.

The results are impressive:

> 1B+ ads processed per second on a single GPU server
> 100x less network traffic through pipeline consolidation
> 300x fewer FLOPs per inference through model redesign

But the most interesting part isn't the raw throughput.

Meta and NVIDIA have optimized a sophisticated Mixture-of-Experts model to run nearly as fast as a simple dot-product scoring kernel.

In other words, Meta can make its ad targeting significantly more intelligent without a proportional increase in serving costs.

For a company generating well over $100B annually from advertising, even a 1% improvement in monetization could translate into billions in additional revenue. And that's before considering infrastructure savings.

For NVIDIA, there's another important takeaway: its competitive advantage extends far beyond the GPUs themselves. Its engineers are working directly with customers to redesign the models, kernels, and execution pipelines running on its hardware.

And Meta says there's still substantial performance headroom, with further optimization already underway for Grace Blackwell.

The real opportunity in AI isn't just building new products. It's making existing businesses more profitable. And NVIDIA is positioning itself at the center of both.

This is the latest iteration of my setup for the Muse Spark Open Kernel Challenge.

The earlier versions ran a small team of long-lived Claudes that decohered after 12 or so hours without hand holding.

I replaced this smorgasbord team with a thin harness. A swarm of 6 (for now) agents now work in parallel, each in its own design lane. 

Every attempt starts as a fresh process that reads two things: the lane's current best kernel, and a shared handoff file of what earlier attempts learned. 

The agents compile and profile on two Nebius spot H200 VMs, but they have no access to the judge. The judge runs the official evaluator inside the SGLang container and times three kernels side by side: the candidate, the lane's current best, and SGLang's own kernel. 

A change is kept only when it passes noise, timing, and compliance. 

A Claude Opus Extra session supervises the loop. It submits every decoder-layer keep to the official board and restarts any spot box after a preemption.

In its first 18 hours the loop made 153 attempts and kept 37 of them. Our overall rank went from #144 to #42. 

Independently, I have a research agent running that looks for implementations, papers, tweets, hints, etc, from publicly available internet sources. 

Most of the gains came from porting kernels that had already been measured in one lane or board into another, and from stacking small improvements. 

Of the first 35 keeps, 24 were ports or combinations, and so far none has come from rewriting a main kernel from scratch.

Climbing up… 

- Claude supervisor with 4 workers 
- Codex supervisor talking to Claude and 4 workers 
- Deepseek swarm of 8 workers. 
- Parametrized optimizer using Clef (I think works ok)
- 3 Nebius spot H200s
- Shared lineage document 
- Constant incessant steering and facepalming

Got 1.569× vs SGLang on the Muse Spark Open Kernel Challenge (bf16 projections, H200). Here’s what worked 

1. At batch sizes of 1–32, the GPU mostly waits on memory, not maths. So the goal is reading fewer bytes.

2. BF16 weights are compressible: the exponents cluster. We store them losslessly in about 12 bits instead of 16 and decode on the fly inside the kernel. Exact same output, about 25% less memory traffic.

3. For small batches I built on the open-source kernels from @alygg77, @vjeux and Nathan Fernandes. Huge credit to them.

4. For batches of 128–256, compression stops helping, so I added my own TMA/wgmma kernel, pinned cuBLASLt configs and a special FP32 router path.

5. An auto-tuner times every option per layer and batch size under CUDA graphs and picks the fastest. Final: 1.569×.

SGLANG 44: Kernels - IV

Saturating NVLink-C2C.

For Hopper or newer cards, SGLang switches to TMA for loads instead of the register kernels from the previous tweet. It maintains a 192 KB ring per block in 6 slots of 32 KB and keeps filling and emptying them asynchronously. ~200 KB per block requirement rules out 5090 even though it is Blackwell. Once the data is loaded into SMEM, it then uses either regular threads (for scattered dst) or TMA bulk store (for contiguous dst) to move it to the destination. This keeps more bytes in flight, as the kernel doesn't need register staging (that is limited by register capacity) and directly moves the data to SMEM. Even though it keeps 3x more bytes in flight, it is only slightly faster than plain threads end to end because of the limits on SM write port speed and TMA bulk op issue rate. One thing PR mentions is that doubling the loads per thread reduces max throughput (paradoxically) due to reduced occupancy but in my testing, even with simple thread loads (outside SGLang), fewer threads x more loads is slower than more threads x fewer loads for the same bytes in flight (this was over PCIe). Not sure why. Measurements below are from the PR desc, it also goes into other details about the kernel.

More details from live demo & third-party benchmarks (Shanghai INESA / Wallstreetcn):

-  Iluvatar says the Tiangai series has already hit 10,000-card cluster deployments.

-  Their Tongyang TY1200 edge chip also beat Nvidia's Thor T5000 by 20% in LLM tests, and the company previously claimed it aims to surpass Nvidia's Rubin architecture within 2 years.

🚨NVFP4不是通用量化，是芯片‑模型深度绑定的产物！

传统通用量化是一套权重跑全部显卡，往往压缩越高，长上下文、Agent推理能力跳水越严重。

NVFP4这套方案完全面向Blackwell硬件指令集定制，做分层差异化量化，牺牲非专家层压缩率，保住模型的复杂推理能力。

这件事释放一个明确信号：未来前沿大模型的落地，基座能力只是一半，芯片厂商深度介入后量化、推理链路调优会成为常态。

代价同样明显，它形成很强硬件绑定，这套高性能权重无法向下兼容Hopper。

往后大模型比拼，不止看论文跑分，硬件‑模型联合优化的工程能力差距会越拉越大。
